newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Leading Russian shares in New Year rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Leading Russian shares in New Year rally.

text.p: Russia's equities market opened the New Year with a bang as leading shares set record highs on Wednesday, and securities analysts predicted prices would advance throughout the month, despite likely corrections.
Utility Mosenergo, one of the most liquid stocks in Russia, touched a record high of $1.220, rising from a close of $1.105 on Monday, the previous trading day.

"People are going for liquidity but most of the money is going into stories that make sense," said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, pointing to Mosenergo and Surgutneftegaz oil companies.
Both have made investment by foreigners and financial transparency company priorities.

Surgut, which on Monday announced details of plans for American Depositary Receipts, which allow foreign investors to buy shares while avoiding domestic settlement problems, hit an intra-day high of $0.585, up from $0.530 at Monday's close.

Experienced and new investors in Russian equities were seen taking part in the bull market, which began over the Christmas and New Year holiday in thin trading and burst to near-record volume of $40 million on Monday.

The Russian Trading System 24-share index rose 16 percent between December 26 and Monday, January 6, partly on mark-ups by domestic brokers, closing at 219.86, just shy of the record 227.79 on July 4.
The International Finance Corporation said Russia was the top emerging market performer in 1996, with a 155.9 percent return in dollar terms.

Analysts said investors, including major new players such as U.S. pension funds, were investing chiefly among leading shares rather than secondary stocks which saw the strongest appreciation towards the end of 1996.
"People are going back to blue chips to get their core positions invested. After that people will start looking around again," Nail said.
But many dealers said a general rally would begin in the second half of January, after a correction among leading issues.
"The question is, who will get nervous first -- those who have not put money in, or those who have the positions," said an analyst at a Western bank in Moscow.

"In the past, the Russians (with the positions) gave in first. I think we will see healthy demand, but not at these levels," he said, predicting leading stocks would ease four to five percent before a general market rally began.
Investors seem confident in Russia politically and economically, and increasingly willing to heed official statements, the analysts said.

The market, repeatedly rocked by rumours in the second half of 1996 that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had died, shrugged off presidential press service statements on Monday and Wednesday that Yeltsin had a cold.
"Unlike communist times, a president's cold does not mean he has been dead for three weeks," said Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Troika-Dialog bank in Moscow.
"Things like Yeltsin's cold will only deter a marginal investor."
